## Applied Exercises

Work on these exercises in CharlesRiver_Work.sqlite, and save the queries of each exercise in a script of its own, named after the exercise (such as `Ex 12.1.sql`). Give each script the structure of the audit query library: a header comment, then one test after another, each under a comment that names it and states its population and expected result. Record a disposition for every exception you find.

### Financial Accounting Exercises

**Exercise 12.1: Cutoff at Each Year-End**

**Table group:** Order-to-Cash, Procure-to-Pay, Payroll, Accounting Core

**Scenario.** Tutorial 12.1 found revenue and payroll recorded in a later fiscal year than the events behind them. The controller asks for the effect on each year's revenue, payroll cost, and year-end liabilities, and for the same test on the supplier side, before the fiscal 2026 statements are finalized.

**Requirements.**

(1) List the sales invoices whose revenue was posted in a different fiscal year from the delivery of the goods they bill, with their SubTotal, invoice date, shipment and delivery dates, and posting date, and list separately the invoices dated before their shipment.

(2) For each fiscal year, total the SubTotal of the revenue recorded in that year for goods delivered in the year before, and of the revenue for goods delivered in that year but recorded in the next one. Add the shipments of fiscal 2026 that were never invoiced, valued at their order price, and calculate the net effect of cutoff on each year's revenue. Explain why the effect on gross margin is larger than the effect on cost of goods sold.

(3) Repeat the test for supplier invoices, comparing InvoiceDate with the posting date of each invoice's ledger rows. Compare the posting dates with ReceivedDate, and explain which date Charles River posts supplier invoices on.

(4) Total the hourly labor cost of LaborTimeEntry (ExtendedLaborCost) by the year of its WorkDate and the fiscal year of its pay period, and identify the cost of work done in December that was recorded in the next fiscal year. Estimate the full payroll cost of the work of 14 to 31 December 2026, whose pay periods have no registers, from the average cost of the last pay periods of fiscal 2026.

(5) Write a short memo (one half page) to the controller with the effect on each year and a recommendation for the year-end close.

**Deliverable.** A script with the cutoff tests and a half-page memo.

**Exercise 12.2: The Accrual for Goods Received Not Invoiced**

**Table group:** Procure-to-Pay, Accounting Core

**Scenario.** Tutorial 12.2 reconciled the receipts not yet invoiced to account 2020 in total. The controller asks for the detail behind the balance at the end of fiscal 2026: which suppliers it is owed to, how old the receipts are, and which purchases are billed without a purchase order at all.

**Requirements.**

(1) List the goods receipt lines not fully invoiced at the end of fiscal 2026, valued at their receipt value for the part not yet invoiced, with the supplier and the receipt date. Bound the receipts and the invoices by date, so that the test could be rerun at another year-end.

(2) Total the value by supplier and list the five largest, and total it by receipt month.

(3) Identify the receipts more than two months old at the year-end, received before 2026-11-01, and suggest why each might not yet be invoiced.

(4) Find the supplier invoice lines that have no purchase order line. Total them by item group, and check whether each is linked to an accrual journal entry. Explain how these purchases should be tested, since a three-way match cannot apply to them.

(5) Write a short memo (one half page) to the controller on the accrual and the purchases without orders.

**Deliverable.** A script with the accrual detail and a half-page memo.

### Managerial Accounting Exercises

**Exercise 12.3: Where Did the Time Go?**

**Table group:** Manufacturing

**Scenario.** Tutorial 11.2 showed Packing and Quality Assurance recording several times their planned hours, and Tutorial 12.3 showed that much of the time was recorded after operations had ended, and that the months of 2024 with almost no indirect time are complete. The plant manager asks what the work-center comparison looks like when only the time recorded while each operation was open is counted, and what the plant was doing in the first months of 2024.

**Requirements.**

(1) For each direct labor time entry, flag whether it was recorded on or before the operation's ActualEndDate.

(2) Repeat the work-center comparison of Tutorial 11.2, with the planned hours of each work center and year, and two recorded-to-planned ratios: one for all direct hours, and one for the hours recorded while the operation was open.

(3) Rank the work centers by each ratio, and describe how the ranking changes.

(4) For each month from January to July 2024, count the work orders released and total the units completed and the manufactured units shipped. Explain why indirect time is almost absent from February to May 2024, and find the month in which the share of direct time recorded after its operation ended first passed a quarter.

(5) Write a short memo (one half page) to the plant manager: what the operation-level data can and cannot support, and what should change in how time is recorded.

**Deliverable.** A script with the comparison and a half-page memo.

**Exercise 12.4: Is the Overtime Approval Doing Its Job?**

**Table group:** Manufacturing, Payroll

**Scenario.** Tutorial 12.3 found that overtime above half an hour is almost always approved, and that most of the growth in overtime sits on days on which every manufacturing employee clocked the same hours. The controller wants to know whether the approvals are a real control over the growth in overtime, or only a record that it happened.

**Requirements.**

(1) Count the overtime approvals by year and reason code, and describe how the mix of reasons changed as overtime grew.

(2) Count the approvals by approver and job title, and calculate the share approved by the largest approver.

(3) Compare each approval's ApprovedHours with its RequestedHours, and its ApprovedDate with the WorkDate of the overtime.

(4) For the surge days of Tutorial 12.3, report who approved the overtime and when, and compare the overtime on those days with the overtime on other days in each year.

(5) Explain what the results say about the design of the overtime approval control, and suggest two changes that would make it a real control.

**Deliverable.** A script with the analysis and a short list of findings and recommendations.

<!-- Instructor notes, Exercise 12.4: 18,145 approvals, spread almost evenly over four reason codes in every year (Backlog Recovery, Late
     Operation, Load Surge, Month-End Support; about a quarter each), so the reasons carry no information about why overtime grew. The
     Production Manager approved 16,676 approvals (about 92%). Every approval grants exactly the hours requested, and every approval is
     dated on the work date itself, so no request was ever reduced or approved in advance. All 5,952 clock entries of the 93 surge days
     were approved by the Production Manager on the work date. Manufacturing overtime on other days stayed about the same (6,273, 6,426,
     5,918 hours), while overtime on surge days grew from 3,456 to 9,216 and 14,112 hours: all the growth. The control records overtime
     rather than authorizing it: approval in advance, a limit per employee and week, and informative reasons reviewed by someone outside
     production would make it a control. -->


### Auditing Exercises

**Exercise 12.5: Duplicate Payments in SQL**

**Table group:** Procure-to-Pay

**Scenario.** Chapter 2 promised that the duplicate payment analysis of Exercise 2.6 would be completed in SQL, and Exercise 8.5 ran the near-duplicate test in Excel. The chief audit executive asks you to confirm those results in SQL on the supplier payments and invoices of fiscal 2024 through 2026, and to add the tests to the query library.

**Requirements.**

(1) Find the supplier invoice numbers that appear more than once for the same supplier, and list both invoices of each pair with their amounts and payments.

(2) Exercise 2.6 warned that the same invoice could be entered with a slightly different number. Repeat test (1) on standardized invoice numbers, using UPPER, TRIM, and REPLACE to remove differences of case, spaces, and hyphens, and report whether it finds any pair that the exact test missed.

(3) Find the check numbers used more than once for the same supplier.

(4) Use a self-join to find pairs of payments to the same supplier for the same amount on different dates within 30 days of each other, dated through 2026-12-31. Report whether any pair pays the same invoice.

(5) For each test, record the number of exceptions and a disposition, and explain why a self-join is needed for the fourth test but not for the others.

**Deliverable.** A script with the four tests and a table of results and dispositions.

<!-- Instructor notes, Exercise 12.5: (1) six supplier invoice numbers each appear twice for the same supplier; each pair has different

     find the same six pairs and no others: the numbers are entered consistently. (3) Two check numbers are used twice, both for
     supplier 1: CHK0006076 and CHK0019708 (the AnomalyLog lists six duplicate references, but only two have check numbers). (4) 113 pairs

     same invoice, so they are recurring purchases rather than duplicates. Grouping finds identical values; comparing each payment with
     other payments across a range of dates needs the table joined to itself. -->


**Exercise 12.6: Sequence and First-Digit Tests in SQL**

**Table group:** Order-to-Cash, Procure-to-Pay, Accounting Core

**Scenario.** The chief audit executive wants the sequence and first-digit tests of Chapter 8 in the query library, so that they run on every document series each quarter without a workbook.

**Requirements.**

(1) For the sales invoice, purchase order, cash receipt, and journal entry numbers, extract the year and the sequence number with SUBSTR and CAST, and report the first and last number of each year.

(2) Describe which series restart their numbering each year and which continue across years.

(3) Use LAG to find any step greater than one: partitioned by year for a series that restarts each year, and ordered across the years, without a partition, for a series that continues, so that a gap at a year boundary is not missed.

(4) Calculate the first significant digit of every supplier payment dated through 2026-12-31 with `printf('%e', Amount)`, and the actual and expected proportion of each digit, using `LOG10(1 + 1.0 / Digit)`.

(5) Calculate the mean absolute deviation for all payments, for full payments (Amount equal to the invoice's GrandTotal), and for partial payments, and compare the results with Tutorial 8.1.

(6) Write a short note on the advantage of running these tests in SQL rather than in a workbook.

**Deliverable.** A script with the sequence and first-digit tests and a short note.

     10,467-18,832); journal entries restart each year (1-266, 1-288, 1-297). A LAG partitioned by year on a continuing series would miss a
